title: Development and validation of the SMART-BPPV: a multimedia learning module for BPPV education.
paragraphs: Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV) is the most common cause of peripheral vertigo, accounting for 17–42% of dizziness-related consultations [ 1 ]. Despite effective canalith repositioning procedures, diagnostic and therapeutic errors remain common and are often attributed to limited training and inadequate understanding of vestibular physiology [ 2 ]. Accurate diagnosis requires spatial understanding of semicircular canal orientation and interpretation of characteristic nystagmus, skills that are difficult to acquire through traditional teaching methods.

Conventional teaching relies on static diagrams and brief demonstrations that fail to convey the dynamic three-dimensional nature of otoconial movement. As a result, learners often experience cognitive overload and difficulty translating theoretical knowledge into clinical practice [ 3 ]. Multimedia approaches can improve spatial understanding and procedural learnin. However, few vestibular education tools are developed using structured instructional design or undergo rigorous validation [ 4 – 6 ]. Consequently, unvalidated educational resources may result in inconsistent content quality and limited generalizability across learner populations.

To address this gap, we developed and validated the Structured Modular Approach for Resource-based Teaching for Benign Paroxysmal Positional Vertigo (SMART-BPPV) learning module. This is a self-directed multimedia learning module based on the ADDIE instructional design framework and cognitive multimedia learning principles. This study reports the module development process and evaluates its content and face validity using established quantitative indices.

This methodological study developed and validated the SMART-BPPV module using the ADDIE instructional design framework (Analysis, Design, Development, Implementation, Evaluation) [ 7 ]. This report covers the first three stages and the validation phases, comprising content validation by subject-matter experts and face validity by end-users. The study was conducted at the Sultan Ahmad Shah Medical Centre @ IIUM between January and October 2025 following approval from the IIUM Research Ethics Committee (IREC 2024 − 334). This study followed established validity frameworks, incorporating content and face validity to support the educational use of the module.

The analysis stage identified learner needs, defined learning objectives, and determined appropriate delivery methods [ 7 ]. This was achieved through a literature review and stakeholder discussions. Review of guidelines and relevant literature identified key domains including pathophysiology, diagnostic maneuvers, nystagmus interpretation, and canalith repositioning procedures [ 1 , 8 ].

Based on the analysis, the module was structured around five core domains of BPPV management (Table 1 ). Learning objectives were derived from literature and expert consensus and refined iteratively. Instructional strategies were developed in accordance with Mayer’s Cognitive Theory of Multimedia Learning to support the presentation of information through concise multimedia elements and a structured learning sequence while maintaining clinical relevance [ 9 ].

Content was developed using a structured storyboard and refined iteratively. The module included thirteen short videos demonstrating diagnostic maneuvers and nystagmus patterns, supported by flowcharts and illustrations. Design principles included content segmentation, synchronized narration, and annotated visuals to facilitate understanding [ 9 ]. Instructional videos were recorded in high definition. Embedded prompts reinforced key steps, and playback controls enabled stepwise observation of eye movements. Nystagmus demonstrations were slowed to highlight subtle findings.

The module was optimized for desktop and mobile use and required approximately 90 min to complete. Materials were hosted on Google Sites and Google Classroom. Representative screenshots and algorithms are shown in Figs. 1 and 2 .

Fig. 1 Representative screenshots of the SMART-BPPV module. A Dashboard interface displayed on Google Sites. B Illustrative slide with accompanying explanatory content. C Instructional video demonstrating nystagmus interpretation. D Instructional video demonstrating canalith repositioning maneuvers

Seven experts in otorhinolaryngology and audiology were purposively recruited between November 2024 and April 2025. Experts rated content relevance and clarity using a 4-point ordinal scale. Ratings of 3 and 4 were classified as relevant. Item-level (I-CVI) and scale-level (S-CVI/Ave) content validity indices were calculated. A threshold of 0.83 was used to indicate acceptable validity [ 10 ]. Items below this threshold were revised iteratively based on quantitative results and qualitative feedback.

Thirty medical officers were recruited using convenience sampling between July and October 2025. Inclusion criteria were at least one year of clinical experience, no prior vestibular training, and affiliation with otorhinolaryngology, emergency medicine, or primary care. Written informed consent was obtained from all participants prior to their inclusion in the study.

Face validity was assessed using a four-point Likert scale evaluating the clarity, relevance, and comprehensibility of the module, with response options ranging from 1 (strongly disagree) to 4 (strongly agree). Item-level (I-FVI) and scale-level (S-FVI/Ave) face validity indices were calculated with a threshold of 0.83. Free-text feedback was collected and analyzed using informal descriptive coding to identify recurring themes.

The analysis stage identified five priority domains: (i) BPPV pathophysiology, (ii) clinical signs and symptoms, (iii) diagnostic maneuvers, (iv) nystagmus patterns, and (v) therapeutic maneuvers. Stakeholder discussions confirmed their relevance and identified key challenges, including fragmented learning resources, misconceptions among junior clinicians, and low confidence in performing maneuvers and differentiating peripheral from central causes.

(ii) Describe the physiology of the vestibulo-ocular reflex. (iii) Discuss the pathophysiology of BPPV. Seven experts participated in content validation. The panel included otorhinolaryngologists and audiologists from academic and government institutions. The scale-level content validity index (S-CVI/Ave) was 0.987. At the item level, 29 of 32 items achieved an I-CVI of 1.000. Three items, namely mechanism of canalith jam, Zuma maneuver, and post-maneuver precautions, had I-CVI values of 0.857 (Table 2 ).

Participants rated the module highly for clarity, organization, and relevance. Qualitative feedback highlighted the usefulness of instructional videos, annotated nystagmus demonstrations, and clinical flowcharts. Minor revisions were made, including refinement of diagram alignment and wording.

Using the ADDIE instructional design framework, this study developed the SMART-BPPV module and demonstrated excellent content validity, with high scale- and item-level indices and strong inter-rater agreement. Although Fleiss’ κ was low, this likely reflects the known prevalence paradox associated with near-unanimous ratings. In contrast, prevalence-robust statistics, including Gwet’s AC1 and modified kappa, demonstrated consistently high agreement, supporting the robustness of expert consensus. Reporting both conventional and prevalence-adjusted indices provides a transparent and methodologically rigorous account of inter-rater reliability. Qualitative feedback further informed targeted refinements in content scope, sequencing, terminology, visual presentation, and safety emphasis

Compared with existing multimedia and simulation-based educational tools, the SMART-BPPV module demonstrated content validity comparable to that reported in previously published educational module validation studies. Prior studies typically report strong S-CVI/Ave values but often rely solely on CVI metrics without incorporating chance-corrected agreement measures [ 13 – 17 ]. By integrating CVI with modified kappa and Gwet’s AC1, this study provides a comprehensive assessment of content validity and inter-rater agreement. This strengthens the methodological credibility of the module and aligns with emerging best practices in instrument validation [ 12 ].

All items met the predefined acceptability threshold. However, three topics namely canalith jam, Zuma maneuver, and post-maneuver precautions, received comparatively lower agreement and were refined following qualitative review. For canalith jam, feedback suggested that the concept was difficult to visualize and potentially less relevant for early learners. Despite this, the topic was retained due to its clinical importance in cases of persistent positional nystagmus and resistance to standard repositioning maneuvers [ 18 ]. Revisions focused on simplifying explanations and incorporating schematic illustrations to facilitate conceptual clarity and reduce cognitive load.

For lateral canal BPPV, the Zuma maneuver was selected as the primary instructional technique, with Kurtzer (Gufoni–Appiani) presented as an alternative. This decision was guided by its applicability across both geotropic and apogeotropic variants, as well as its relative simplicity and reproducibility in teaching context [ 19 – 21 ]. While reported success rates vary across studies, likely reflecting differences in patient selection and technique, its mechanistic clarity and suitability for educational purposes support its inclusion as the primary teaching maneuver [ 22 , 23 ]. Post-maneuver precautions were also revised to reflect contemporary evidence, with content emphasizing that routine postural restrictions are not universally required and should be applied selectively [ 1 ]. These refinements highlight the value of integrating quantitative validity measures with qualitative expert feedback during educational resource development, ensuring that the content remains clinically accurate, relevant, and responsive to user needs.

An important consideration in the assessment of patients presenting with positional vertigo is the differentiation of benign peripheral vestibular disorders from central neurological pathology. Central lesions may present with positional vertigo and nystagmus that mimic BPPV, increasing the risk of misdiagnosis and delayed recognition of serious conditions such as posterior circulation stroke [ 24 ]. This is particularly relevant in primary care and emergency settings, where dizziness and vertigo may be the initial or only presenting manifestation of cerebrovascular disease [ 25 ]. To address this challenge, the SMART-BPPV module incorporates dedicated content on distinguishing peripheral and central vertigo, including a comparative clinical features table, instruction on the HINTS examination, recognition of red-flag features, and a clinical algorithm that highlights pathways for suspected central causes and appropriate referral. Although the primary focus of the module is the diagnosis and management of BPPV, these components were incorporated to emphasize safe clinical assessment and support early recognition of patients who may require further neurological evaluation. Future enhancements may further expand content related to central causes of vertigo and their management.

The SMART-BPPV module was developed using established instructional design principles and cognitive multimedia learning theory, incorporating segmented videos, annotated visuals, and structured content progression to facilitate learning of key concepts in BPPV diagnosis and management. Its user-centered design promotes accessibility across varied learning environments. Following systematic development, the module demonstrated excellent content validity and face validity and was refined through expert and end-user feedback. These findings support the appropriateness, clarity, and usability of the module as a structured educational resource for introductory BPPV education. However, while the module includes demonstrations of diagnostic and therapeutic maneuvers, the present study did not evaluate learner outcomes, clinical reasoning, or procedural competence. Given that BPPV assessment and treatment involves psychomotor skills, competency development requires supervised practice, feedback, and clinical experience in addition to educational materials.

Several limitations should be considered. First, the expert panel and participants were drawn from a single national context, which may limit the generalizability of the findings to other healthcare settings. Second, although expert feedback was obtained systematically, a formal Delphi process was not employed, potentially limiting opportunities for iterative consensus building. Third, this study was limited to the evaluation of content validity and face validity and therefore cannot determine the module’s impact on knowledge acquisition, clinical decision-making, or procedural performance. Future research should include learner-based outcome evaluations, such as pre–post educational assessments, objective measures of procedural competence, and multicenter studies to establish the educational effectiveness and broader applicability of the SMART-BPPV module.

The SMART-BPPV module demonstrated excellent content and face validity, with high agreement among experts and end-users, supporting the appropriateness, clarity, and relevance of its content. Developed using the ADDIE framework and informed by cognitive learning theory, the module underwent systematic development and iterative refinement based on expert and end-user feedback. These findings support SMART-BPPV as a validated educational resource for BPPV education and provide a replicable framework for the development of future multimedia learning modules. Future research should evaluate the educational impact of the module on learner knowledge, clinical reasoning, and performance of diagnostic and therapeutic BPPV maneuvers.

Participants rated the module highly for clarity, organization, and relevance. Qualitative feedback highlighted the usefulness of instructional videos, annotated nystagmus demonstrations, and clinical flowcharts. Minor revisions were made, including refinement of diagram alignment and wording.

Using the ADDIE instructional design framework, this study developed the SMART-BPPV module and demonstrated excellent content validity, with high scale- and item-level indices and strong inter-rater agreement. Although Fleiss’ κ was low, this likely reflects the known prevalence paradox associated with near-unanimous ratings. In contrast, prevalence-robust statistics, including Gwet’s AC1 and modified kappa, demonstrated consistently high agreement, supporting the robustness of expert consensus. Reporting both conventional and prevalence-adjusted indices provides a transparent and methodologically rigorous account of inter-rater reliability. Qualitative feedback further informed targeted refinements in content scope, sequencing, terminology, visual presentation, and safety emphasis

Compared with existing multimedia and simulation-based educational tools, the SMART-BPPV module demonstrated content validity comparable to that reported in previously published educational module validation studies. Prior studies typically report strong S-CVI/Ave values but often rely solely on CVI metrics without incorporating chance-corrected agreement measures [ 13 – 17 ]. By integrating CVI with modified kappa and Gwet’s AC1, this study provides a comprehensive assessment of content validity and inter-rater agreement. This strengthens the methodological credibility of the module and aligns with emerging best practices in instrument validation [ 12 ].

All items met the predefined acceptability threshold. However, three topics namely canalith jam, Zuma maneuver, and post-maneuver precautions, received comparatively lower agreement and were refined following qualitative review. For canalith jam, feedback suggested that the concept was difficult to visualize and potentially less relevant for early learners. Despite this, the topic was retained due to its clinical importance in cases of persistent positional nystagmus and resistance to standard repositioning maneuvers [ 18 ]. Revisions focused on simplifying explanations and incorporating schematic illustrations to facilitate conceptual clarity and reduce cognitive load.

For lateral canal BPPV, the Zuma maneuver was selected as the primary instructional technique, with Kurtzer (Gufoni–Appiani) presented as an alternative. This decision was guided by its applicability across both geotropic and apogeotropic variants, as well as its relative simplicity and reproducibility in teaching context [ 19 – 21 ]. While reported success rates vary across studies, likely reflecting differences in patient selection and technique, its mechanistic clarity and suitability for educational purposes support its inclusion as the primary teaching maneuver [ 22 , 23 ]. Post-maneuver precautions were also revised to reflect contemporary evidence, with content emphasizing that routine postural restrictions are not universally required and should be applied selectively [ 1 ]. These refinements highlight the value of integrating quantitative validity measures with qualitative expert feedback during educational resource development, ensuring that the content remains clinically accurate, relevant, and responsive to user needs.

An important consideration in the assessment of patients presenting with positional vertigo is the differentiation of benign peripheral vestibular disorders from central neurological pathology. Central lesions may present with positional vertigo and nystagmus that mimic BPPV, increasing the risk of misdiagnosis and delayed recognition of serious conditions such as posterior circulation stroke [ 24 ]. This is particularly relevant in primary care and emergency settings, where dizziness and vertigo may be the initial or only presenting manifestation of cerebrovascular disease [ 25 ]. To address this challenge, the SMART-BPPV module incorporates dedicated content on distinguishing peripheral and central vertigo, including a comparative clinical features table, instruction on the HINTS examination, recognition of red-flag features, and a clinical algorithm that highlights pathways for suspected central causes and appropriate referral. Although the primary focus of the module is the diagnosis and management of BPPV, these components were incorporated to emphasize safe clinical assessment and support early recognition of patients who may require further neurological evaluation. Future enhancements may further expand content related to central causes of vertigo and their management.

The SMART-BPPV module was developed using established instructional design principles and cognitive multimedia learning theory, incorporating segmented videos, annotated visuals, and structured content progression to facilitate learning of key concepts in BPPV diagnosis and management. Its user-centered design promotes accessibility across varied learning environments. Following systematic development, the module demonstrated excellent content validity and face validity and was refined through expert and end-user feedback. These findings support the appropriateness, clarity, and usability of the module as a structured educational resource for introductory BPPV education. However, while the module includes demonstrations of diagnostic and therapeutic maneuvers, the present study did not evaluate learner outcomes, clinical reasoning, or procedural competence. Given that BPPV assessment and treatment involves psychomotor skills, competency development requires supervised practice, feedback, and clinical experience in addition to educational materials.

Several limitations should be considered. First, the expert panel and participants were drawn from a single national context, which may limit the generalizability of the findings to other healthcare settings. Second, although expert feedback was obtained systematically, a formal Delphi process was not employed, potentially limiting opportunities for iterative consensus building. Third, this study was limited to the evaluation of content validity and face validity and therefore cannot determine the module’s impact on knowledge acquisition, clinical decision-making, or procedural performance. Future research should include learner-based outcome evaluations, such as pre–post educational assessments, objective measures of procedural competence, and multicenter studies to establish the educational effectiveness and broader applicability of the SMART-BPPV module.

The SMART-BPPV module demonstrated excellent content and face validity, with high agreement among experts and end-users, supporting the appropriateness, clarity, and relevance of its content. Developed using the ADDIE framework and informed by cognitive learning theory, the module underwent systematic development and iterative refinement based on expert and end-user feedback. These findings support SMART-BPPV as a validated educational resource for BPPV education and provide a replicable framework for the development of future multimedia learning modules. Future research should evaluate the educational impact of the module on learner knowledge, clinical reasoning, and performance of diagnostic and therapeutic BPPV maneuvers.
